IA-2025-HCR105.s: The resolution would set the agenda for the first extraordinary session of the 2026 Iowa legislative session. It would limit that session to a bill on the major economic growth attraction program, including its effective date, and to any other resolutions either chamber adopts.

IA-2025-HF1028.s: Now that it is law, this act changes several rules for the Iowa Department of Management. It lets the department move money between agencies under set limits, changes how the technology reinvestment fund is used and reported on, and gives it yearly funding for that fund. It also updates background check rules for some workers and bars certain contract terms, like ones that make the department take on another person's debt or let another party change terms on its own.

IA-2025-HF2199.s: The law updates rules for level II law enforcement academy training programs in Iowa. It says people applying through the short-course level II program must show they finished a two-year or four-year police science or criminal justice program, or meet other academy rules, and they must be hired by a law enforcement agency within 18 months after finishing the program if they were not hired already.

IA-2025-HF2200.s: The law changes how Iowa handles alcohol license rules in the Department of Revenue. It sets new limits on when some department leaders and employees can have money ties to alcohol businesses, and it bars them from using their office to push political views or candidates. It also lets certain small investors keep a limited ownership stake in both a wholesale or production business and a retail alcohol business, with yearly disclosure to the department kept private. The act took effect when it was signed.

IA-2025-HF2230.s: Signed into law, this measure changes teacher training and licensing in Iowa. Starting July 1, 2027, teacher prep programs must include more training and practice on teaching students with disabilities and English learners, and students must pass a final end-of-program test for their license area. It also requires people seeking a special education teaching job to complete a state-made self-paced course on special education laws, testing, and key skills before getting a class B or conditional license.

IA-2025-HF2231.s: The law creates a seal of civics excellence program run by the state education department. It lets high school students earn a seal by showing knowledge of American government and taking part in civic and community activities. Schools may join the program if they choose, and the seal can be put on a transcript or diploma. The department may charge a small fee for printing and postage.

IA-2025-HF2254.s: The law bars the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics from putting noncompete clauses in job contracts with certain health workers, including nurses, pharmacists, physicians, and physician assistants. A noncompete clause is a rule that limits where someone can work after a job ends. It applies to contracts entered into, extended, or renewed on or after the law takes effect, which is upon enactment.

IA-2025-HF2356.s: This law creates a state public defender pilot project to try new ways of giving legal help to families in the child welfare system. The project may run in up to 16 counties and may use team-based or other methods, work with other groups, and seek grant money. It also lets the public defender appoint a lawyer before formal court steps in some cases if that fits the project’s goals.

IA-2025-HF2493.s: Now law, this measure changes Iowa’s statewide preschool program for some four- and five-year-olds. It updates who can enroll, how schools count students for state money, and when preschool counts as compulsory attendance unless a parent or guardian opts out in writing. It applies to school budget years starting on or after July 1, 2027.

IA-2025-HF2514.s: This law makes children of some child care workers in Iowa eligible for the state child care help program. It covers workers at licensed child care facilities or homes who meet set work and job rules, and the family must still meet the program’s need test and pay any required copay. The law also requires the department to give lawmakers a yearly report on spending and how many families and children take part.

IA-2025-HF2515.s: The law changes Iowa rules on deferred or suspended sentences, which are sentence options that delay or lessen punishment. It adds cases under section 728.12, which covers sexual exploitation of a minor, to the list of offenses affected. It became law as Chapter 1023.

IA-2025-HF2531.s: The law changes how counties and cities handle mineral interests under land. In most cases, they must give those mineral interests to the surface owner at no cost, with deadlines for older and newly acquired interests. It also changes rules for mineral taxes, tax sales, and when a coal mineral interest is treated as active or abandoned.

IA-2025-HF2591.s: The law changes Iowa rules for open enrollment, student transfers, and school sports eligibility. It lets eighth graders join certain school sports contests on the same basis as high school students, and it sets new waiting periods for some students in grades 9 through 12 who transfer or use open enrollment before they can play varsity sports. The sports rule for eighth graders and the emergency rule steps took effect when the law was enacted, and the other changes took effect on August 1, 2026.

IA-2025-HF2601.s: This law tightens Iowa campaign finance rules for ballot issue campaigns, which are efforts to pass or defeat a measure on the ballot. It bars foreign nationals from taking part in decisions about those campaigns or from asking others to give or spend money for them, and it requires certain donor affirmations in campaign reports. It also sets rules for investigations to protect donor privacy where possible and adds civil penalties of $10,000 or three times the amount involved, whichever is greater.

IA-2025-HF2602.s: The law requires massage establishments to get a license starting January 1, 2027. It lets the board inspect these places, check fingerprints and criminal history, and deny, suspend, or revoke a license for certain problems. It also requires records to be kept for three years and allows fines and other penalties for people or businesses that operate without the right license.

IA-2025-HF2617.s: The law changes Iowa rules for abandoned vehicles. It lets a private towing company accept credit card payment in some release cases, gives owners and lienholders 20 days to reclaim a vehicle after notice, and allows owners to get certain personal items from the vehicle during that time. It also lets lienholders ask to inspect the vehicle for up to a $100 fee and requires private entities to post their storage and impound fees.

IA-2025-HF2667.s: The bill would create a statewide urban design and specifications board in the transportation department to set design and specs manuals for public projects. It would also require the board to post changes and an estimate of any cost changes from those updates. If a county or city approves a project plan that does not follow these standards, the local government would have to pay the extra costs, and property owners could not be billed for those costs.

IA-2025-HF2678.s: The law changes filing rules for partnerships and limited partnerships with the Iowa secretary of state. It lets a person file a sworn statement if their name, address, or email was used without permission, and the secretary of state can remove that information with no fee. It also lets the secretary of state require some filings to be sent by mail or in person when there is credible information they may be fraudulent or used for an unlawful purpose, and it allows written questions to be sent to a partnership in those cases.

IA-2025-HF2706.s: This act changes how Iowa magistrates are appointed and tracked in judicial election districts. It also changes rules for using district associate judges in place of magistrates, how magistrate pay is set, and what court officials must record and report. The law became Chapter 1063 and takes effect on the dates listed in the act.

IA-2025-HF2711.s: The law changes Iowa rules on state programs and jobs that use race or gender-based requirements. It keeps equal-opportunity rules for state agencies, the regents, school districts, area education agencies, and community colleges, and it directs them to use affirmative action steps, training, reporting, and contract rules tied to Iowa-based businesses. It also gives the Department of Administrative Services and the Board of Regents duties to oversee these efforts and report on them.

IA-2025-HF2756.s: Iowa now requires service companies to be licensed before they can sell motor vehicle or residential service contracts in the state. It sets rules for license applications, renewals, reporting changes, and fees, and says these contracts are not insurance. The law also allows civil penalties and includes effective date provisions.

IA-2025-HF2757.s: The law creates sales and use tax breaks and refunds for nuclear electric generation facilities for work like site prep, construction, repairs, safe storage, and restarting a shut-down plant. It also sets up a state fund for nuclear energy workforce programs at state colleges and gives money to the Board of Regents for those programs. A facility that uses the tax break must make yearly payments to the fund and may have to repay the tax savings if it does not start or restart commercial operation within the set time.

IA-2025-HF2765.s: Iowa law now adds rules for mining land that is affected by subsidence, which means land sinking or collapsing above an underground mine on public land or in a public right-of-way. It directs the state to make rules for reporting these cases, who can file a repair plan, and how soon repairs must be done. The law also says the state must adopt emergency rules within 60 business days after it took effect, and it took effect when it was enacted.

IA-2025-HF2769.s: The law gives money to the judicial branch for the fiscal year starting July 1, 2026, including funds for court staff, jury and witness fees, juvenile court services, juvenile sanctions, and a possible business court. It also sets rules for how the branch must report spending, collect fines and court costs, and use state budget and payroll systems. For that same year, it lets civil trials move to a nearby county if all parties agree, allows some travel pay to be waived, and lets judicial officers be placed on unpaid leave when branch workers are on temporary layoff.

IA-2025-HF2772.s: The law sets state funding for economic development programs for the fiscal year starting July 1, 2026. It gives money to the Economic Development Authority, including $12,903,510 for its work, $450,000 for the World Food Prize, $1,050,000 for the tourism office, and $1,601,800 for Iowa arts council support. It also codifies, or puts into law, the Housing Renewal Program and became law on June 2, 2026.

IA-2025-HF2782.s: This became law and sets state funding for the Iowa Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Health and Human Services for the 2026-27 year. It covers programs for aging and disability services, behavioral health, public health, Hawki, medical aid, family support, and other health services. It also sets money and reporting rules for some programs, and the governor vetoed some parts before signing the rest.

IA-2025-HF2783.s: This law sets state money for the education system for the fiscal year that starts July 1, 2026. It covers funding for the Department for the Blind, the Department of Education, the Board of Regents, the Department of Workforce Development, and the Iowa Special Education Council. The governor approved the rest of the bill but vetoed one item in a section about school cybersecurity services.

IA-2025-HF2788.s: Iowa's new law changes how abortion is defined and adds new rules for informed consent. It requires an in-person exam before an abortion, adds steps and warnings before abortion drugs are prescribed or given, and limits where those drugs can be dispensed. It also creates civil liability and license discipline for people who violate the drug rules, and it changes what must be reported about abortions and miscarriages.

IA-2025-HF2794.s: This law creates a grant program in the Iowa Department of Justice to help sexual assault forensic examination centers. It lets the attorney general hire a qualifying Iowa nonprofit to run and maintain these centers, and that group must provide care, training, and reports on services. The law also creates a trust fund for gifts, grants, and other money to pay for the program and grants to these centers.

IA-2025-HF2799.s: The act changes programs under the economic development authority, the utilities commission, and the department of education. It creates a new headquarters expansion and growth program and a business training fund, and it repeals some older tax credit and training programs. It also changes electric transmission planning and creates a new fund for that work, and it sets up an interim study committee on job training.

IA-2025-HF2801.s: The bill would change Iowa’s major economic growth attraction program, which offers tax credits to some businesses for big investment projects. It would set new site rules, including a larger site size for some projects and a special tax credit for one eligible business in a rural county, which it defines as a county with 50,000 people or less. It would also change when credits can be claimed, allow some rural county credits to be transferred, and let the state or county seek repayment if a business breaks the program rules.

IA-2025-HF571.s: Becomes law in Iowa as the Medical Ethics Defense Act. It protects medical practitioners and health care institutions from certain penalties or discrimination when they refuse to take part in care for conscience reasons, report possible violations, or engage in speech or other protected expression. It also sets rules for complaints and can fine a licensing or certifying agency $500 per day if it does not share a complaint within 21 days.

IA-2025-HF917.s: As law, this measure creates rules on lawsuits against motocross facilities in Iowa. It says a facility is not liable for injuries or death from the normal risks of motocross, like rider error, bad weather, animals, or remote locations without medical care. It also keeps liability in place for intentional harm, negligence, unsafe gear, or failing to use proper care, and it requires warning signs at the facility.

IA-2025-HF990.s: The law changes Iowa rules for medical cannabidiol registration cards and for licensing medical cannabidiol dispensaries. It removes one filing detail for patient cards, updates the patient information that must be listed, and lets the state health department license medical cannabidiol dispensaries each year. It affects patients who use medical cannabidiol and the dispensaries that sell it.

IA-2025-HSB785.s: The bill would change Iowa’s major economic growth attraction program for business projects that get tax credits. It would add a special tax credit for one eligible business in a rural county, allow some of these credits to be transferred to another person or company with state approval, and set rules for repayment if the business does not follow the program. It also would define terms like “rural county” and “affiliate,” and it includes effective date provisions.

IA-2025-SCR103.s: The resolution would set the agenda for Iowa’s first extra legislative session in 2026. It would limit that session to a bill on the major economic growth attraction program, plus any other resolutions either chamber adopts.

IA-2025-SF2039.s: This law lets certain leaders in the Iowa General Assembly ask to join court cases that review decisions made by state agencies. Other lawmakers may join a request to intervene, which means to take part in the case. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

IA-2025-SF2086.s: The law lets school districts and accredited nonpublic schools offer an elective junior fire fighter program to students in grades 11 and 12. The program must work with a local fire department and use training and curriculum approved by the fire service training bureau. It also sets what students under 18 may do and what they may not do, and it lets students who finish the program and meet other requirements take firefighter I certification testing, though the certification is not issued until age 18.

IA-2025-SF2189.s: This law changes the information nonresidents must give when they apply to register a vehicle or get an Iowa title. It requires the application to include the primary user’s name, Iowa driver’s license or nonoperator ID number, birth date, residence, and mailing address, or the business’s address and federal tax ID if the user is a business. For a nonresident who owns Iowa property and mainly uses the vehicle there, the application may use proof of property ownership and may use an out-of-state driver’s license or ID number instead of some of the Iowa information. The state agency must set rules for what counts as proof of property ownership.

IA-2025-SF2201.s: Iowa enacted a school funding law for the budget year starting July 1, 2026. It sets the state growth rate at 2% and changes how some school aid is figured, including property tax replacement payments and transportation equity aid. The law also moves school district budget adjustment funding to state foundation aid and creates a salary supplement for education support staff.

IA-2025-SF2218.s: The law changes school licensing rules so the board of educational examiners must check identity and work eligibility for new license applicants and renewals, and some practitioners must prove work eligibility every five years. It also bars employers from keeping workers they know used a social security number that is not theirs, sets a $10,000 civil penalty, and adds criminal penalties for false use of a social security number. In addition, it requires e-verify checks for newly hired employees in parts of state government, with a way for workers to challenge the result.

IA-2025-SF2220.s: The law changes Iowa school rules for student testing, gifted and talented programs, advanced math, and course acceleration. It requires school districts to set up clearer ways to find and serve gifted and talented children, build an advanced math path, and create rules for subject and whole-grade acceleration and for automatic placement into more advanced classes for some students. It also says the state cost of these new rules must be paid from school foundation aid sent to districts.

IA-2025-SF2231.s: Iowa enacted a law that changes school rules on student speech and religious expression, and it requires the education department to share federal guidance and model policies with schools. It also changes preschool program rules for four-year-old children and sets new rules for some charter schools and innovation zone schools to follow the same protected speech standards as school districts. The law also updates some college credit and shared-time education program rules for high school students.

IA-2025-SF2289.s: The act changes rules for gambling, state building codes, and certain residential care facilities. It lets the state gambling commission take more enforcement steps, changes some tax withholding rules on gambling winnings, and says part of that tax change takes effect right away. It also updates rules for safe rooms and storm shelters in the building code, and creates a special class of residential care facilities for pediatric palliative care patients that only provide respite care and hospice services.

IA-2025-SF2304.s: Became law in Iowa. It lets water and wastewater utilities seek special rate charges to recover costs for certain infrastructure work, such as new required facilities, relocations, and other nonrevenue projects needed for health, safety, resilience, or environmental protection. Utilities must first get commission approval for a plan, and the law sets filing, review, and cost limit rules for those charges.

IA-2025-SF2422.s: The law changes rules for state public assistance programs, including SNAP, Medicaid, and the Iowa Health and Wellness Plan. It updates how the state checks citizenship and immigration status, changes SNAP income and eligibility rules for some noncitizens, and requires reports on SNAP payment error rates starting in the fiscal quarter that begins October 1, 2026. It also directs the department to seek federal waivers for SNAP benefit timing and verification rules, and changes Medicaid retroactive coverage rules for some people, with some parts taking effect January 1, 2027.

IA-2025-SF2426.s: The law adds English-language checks for people who apply for or renew a commercial driver’s license or commercial learner’s permit in Iowa. Drivers who cannot show enough English skill may be denied a license or permit, and people who do not meet the rule may not operate a commercial vehicle; the law also sets penalties for drivers and motor carriers that violate it. The new license check starts on March 1, 2027, or when the transportation department says its new records system is ready, whichever comes first.

IA-2025-SF2428.s: The law changes Iowa school rules on student discipline, special education, and staff duties. It affects school districts, charter schools, innovation zone schools, teachers, and students with special education plans or plans under section 504 of the federal Rehabilitation Act. It also orders the education department to make training on special education team rules, creates a pilot program for one rural and one urban district, and lets teachers ask for a student’s special education team meeting.

IA-2025-SF2429.s: The law lets the state issue yearly permits for vehicles hauling fluid milk products to or from a milk plant, receiving station, or transfer station. It allows those vehicles to go over the usual weight limit, up to 136,000 pounds, on primary roads and primary road extensions in cities. The Transportation Department must set rules for minimum distances between axles, and the law takes effect January 1, 2027.

IA-2025-SF2453.s: The bill would have required Iowa’s public universities to invest at least 1% of their endowment assets in certified innovation funds by July 1, 2027. It would have let the regents grant a one-year waiver and could have cut some state funding if an institution did not comply. The bill would also have required yearly reports and a public list of eligible funds, and it was vetoed by the governor.

IA-2025-SF2480.s: The law changes Iowa rules for alternative nicotine products and vapor products, which are nicotine items that are not tobacco. It adds new taxes on these products, set at 5 cents per container for alternative nicotine products and 5 cents per milliliter for vapor products, and it updates who is treated as a distributor, manufacturer, or seller for tax purposes. It also sets aside the first $3 million each year from these new taxes, starting July 1, 2027, for pediatric cancer research and related care at the University of Iowa Stead Family Children's Hospital.

IA-2025-SF2484.s: This Iowa law makes money available for several state funds and projects in fiscal year 2026-2027. It includes funding for road and building work, water quality programs, farm fertilizer planning tools, and tourism-related funds. It also changes who can get some kinds of financial help, including regional sports authority districts and groups tied to major events, tourism, and sports tourism. The governor signed the bill but vetoed one part that would have limited some large health and human services technology contracts.

IA-2025-SF2488.s: The law creates a statewide early childhood and family services system for children under 19 and their families, run by the state health and human services department. It sets up district plans and advisory councils, and it directs the department to use services such as family support, early help, and community resources to support healthy child development. It also includes money for the program and creates an interim study committee to review early childhood Iowa issues.

IA-2025-SF2490.s: The law changes Iowa rules for oil and gas production, including filing papers with the Department of Natural Resources, shared drilling plans, and how confidential records are handled. It creates a severance tax account in the Environment First Fund, and money in it is to support water quality projects. It also lets the department set special spacing units for exploratory wells and gives civil penalties for violations.

IA-2025-SF2493.s: This law exempts some ethanol-blended gasoline from Iowa’s excise tax when it is bought for use only in an implement of husbandry used in farm production. Buyers must use a state exemption certificate, and suppliers must keep it for at least three years. If the fuel is later used in a nonexempt way, the buyer must pay the tax directly to the state.

IA-2025-SF2508.s: The bill would change Iowa’s major economic growth attraction program. It would add new rules for where projects must be located, raise the tax credit to up to 10% for one project in a rural county, and let some rural county credits be refundable and transferred to another person with approval. It would also tighten repayment rules if a business breaks program rules and add penalties if a project’s land or buildings are sold, razed, or made unusable within five years.

IA-2025-SF378.s: The law changes how some speeding tickets are counted for driver records, probation decisions, and car insurance rates. It raises the default speed limit for all vehicle traffic from 55 to 60 miles per hour, unless another speed limit applies, and expands the speed zones covered by the rule to 34 to 61 miles per hour. It also lets road agencies use temporary stickers or overlays on existing signs when posting the new speed limits, and it became law in Iowa as Chapter 1132.

IA-2025-SF472.s: The law changes when Iowa holds retention and recertification elections for public employee bargaining units. It sets election windows before a contract ends and requires public employers to send the board a list of unit employees, with a court process to compel that list if needed. The law takes effect right away and applies to election notices issued on or after that date.

IA-2025-SF473.s: The law changes child foster care and adoption rules for some people and groups with sincere religious or moral beliefs about sexual orientation or gender identity. It says the state cannot require certain foster caregivers or adoptive parents to agree with beliefs that conflict with their own, and it lets them sue or ask the attorney general to enforce the rule. It also says religious groups that work with the state on foster care or adoption cannot be forced to provide those services in a way that conflicts with their beliefs, while the state still must look at a child’s best interests.

IA-2025-SF512.s: The act changes Iowa law on time limits for filing civil lawsuits. It says the rule for when a claim starts, including the discovery rule and similar rules, stays in place, and that any change to those time limits can only be made by the General Assembly.

IA-2025-SF629.s: This act creates an optional fast-track filing service for business documents handled by the Iowa secretary of state. The added surcharge is $200 for one hour, $125 for same day, $50 for two days, or $15 for five days, on top of the normal filing fee. The secretary must give written proof of the filing, and the extra money goes to the business administration fund.

IA-2025-SF654.s: Iowa enacted a law on wildlife rules for beaver dams, tree stands, traps, snares, fur dealer licenses, and deer damage permits. It requires ID tags on tree stands on public land, sets rules for tags and checks on traps and snares, and lets owners or drainage districts alter beaver dams to protect property. It also caps fur dealer license fees at $50 a year and keeps deer depredation permits available for landowners or tenants with at least $1,000 in wildlife damage.
